We studied experimentally the role of phonon dimensionality on electron-phonon (e-p) interaction in thin copper wires evaporated either on suspended silicon nitride membranes or on bulk substrates, at sub-Kelvin temperatures. The power emitted from electrons to phonons was measured using sensitive normal metal-insulator-superconductor (NIS) tunnel junction thermometers. Membrane thicknesses ranging from 30 nm to 750 nm were used to clearly see the onset of the effects of two-dimensional (2D) phonon system. We observed for the first time that a 2D phonon spectrum clearly changes the temperature dependence and strength of the e-p scattering rate, with the interaction becoming stronger at the lowest temperatures below $\sim$ 0.5 K for the 30 nm membranes.

# Phonon Dimensionality and Electron-Phonon Interaction in Thin Copper Wires

## Overview

This study presents an experimental investigation into how the dimensionality of phonons influences electron-phonon interaction in thin copper wires at sub-Kelvin temperatures. Understanding this fundamental interaction is crucial, as it governs heat transfer processes in nanoscale systems and becomes particularly significant at very low temperatures, where the behavior of phonons can deviate from conventional three-dimensional predictions.

## Experimental Methods

To probe the electron-phonon coupling, the researchers measured the power transferred from electrons to phonons using highly sensitive normal metal–insulator–superconductor (NIS) tunnel junction thermometers. These NIS junctions provide precise temperature measurements at the sub-Kelvin scale, enabling accurate quantification of the thermal energy exchanged between the electron and phonon subsystems.

A key aspect of the experimental design involved the use of silicon nitride membranes with thicknesses ranging from 30 nm to 750 nm. By systematically varying the membrane thickness, the team was able to observe the onset of two-dimensional phonon system effects. As the membrane becomes sufficiently thin, the phonon spectrum transitions from a three-dimensional to a two-dimensional character, allowing the researchers to directly study the consequences of reduced phonon dimensionality.

## Key Findings

The most significant result of this work is the first experimental observation that a two-dimensional phonon spectrum alters both the temperature dependence and the strength of the electron-phonon scattering rate. This demonstrates that phonon dimensionality is not merely a theoretical consideration but has measurable physical consequences for energy relaxation in nanoscale conductors.

Specifically, the researchers found that the electron-phonon interaction became stronger at the lowest temperatures—below approximately 0.5 K—for the thinnest 30 nm membranes. This enhancement of coupling in the low-temperature, two-dimensional regime highlights how geometric confinement of phonons can fundamentally modify the thermal properties of metallic nanostructures.

## Significance

These findings provide important insight into the role of dimensionality in electron-phonon physics and have practical implications for the design of low-temperature nanoscale devices, such as radiation detectors and quantum circuits, where controlling heat flow between electrons and phonons is essential for optimal performance.

# Phonon Dimensionality and Electron-Phonon Interaction in Thin Copper Wires

## Introduction and Motivation

The electron-phonon interaction represents one of the most fundamental coupling mechanisms in condensed matter physics, governing the exchange of energy between the electronic and lattice degrees of freedom in metals. At sub-Kelvin temperatures, this interaction becomes the dominant channel through which electrons in a conductor thermally equilibrate with their surroundings, and it plays a decisive role in the operation of a wide range of cryogenic devices, including superconducting detectors, bolometers, and quantum circuits. While the behavior of electron-phonon coupling in bulk three-dimensional materials has been extensively characterized, its behavior when the phonon environment itself is spatially confined has remained comparatively poorly understood.

When a metallic conductor is deposited on an extremely thin dielectric membrane, the phonon spectrum of the supporting structure can be modified. If the membrane thickness becomes comparable to or smaller than the characteristic thermal phonon wavelength, the phonon modes may no longer be described by a fully three-dimensional density of states. Instead, the reduced dimensionality restricts the available phonon modes, effectively producing a two-dimensional phonon spectrum. This dimensional crossover is expected to alter both the temperature scaling and the overall magnitude of the electron-phonon scattering rate—yet direct experimental verification of these effects has been lacking.

## Experimental Approach

To address this open question, researchers carried out a systematic experimental investigation of how phonon dimensionality influences the electron-phonon interaction. The central experimental platform consisted of thin copper wires deposited onto suspended silicon nitride membranes whose thicknesses were varied over a broad range, spanning from 30 nanometers up to 750 nanometers. For comparison and to establish a reference case corresponding to conventional three-dimensional phonon behavior, additional copper wires were fabricated directly on bulk substrates.

The key experimental quantity of interest was the rate of power emission from the electron system to the phonon system. To access this quantity with the required precision at sub-Kelvin temperatures, the researchers employed normal metal–insulator–superconductor (NIS) tunnel junctions as sensitive thermometers. These junctions exploit the strongly temperature-dependent tunneling characteristics across the superconducting energy gap, enabling accurate measurement of the local electron temperature within the copper wires. By deliberately heating the electron gas and monitoring the resulting steady-state electron temperature as a function of injected power and bath temperature, the electron-to-phonon power flow could be extracted directly.

## Principal Findings

The measurements provided the first clear experimental demonstration that a two-dimensional phonon spectrum modifies the electron-phonon interaction in two distinct respects. First, the temperature dependence of the electron-phonon scattering rate was found to deviate from the behavior expected for a bulk three-dimensional phonon environment. Second, the overall strength, or magnitude, of the coupling was altered by the dimensional confinement of the phonons.

Most notably, for the thinnest membranes—those with a thickness of only 30 nanometers—the electron-phonon interaction became significantly stronger below a temperature of approximately 0.5 K. In this regime, the reduced membrane thickness confines the relevant thermal phonons to two dimensions, and the resulting enhancement of the coupling represents a direct signature of the phonon dimensional crossover. In contrast, the wires fabricated on thicker membranes and on bulk substrates exhibited behavior consistent with a fully three-dimensional phonon spectrum, confirming that the observed effects were genuinely attributable to the reduced dimensionality of the phonon environment.

## Significance

These results carry both fundamental and practical importance. From a fundamental standpoint, they establish experimentally that phonon dimensionality is a controllable parameter that reshapes electron-phonon energy exchange, offering a route to test and refine theoretical models of reduced-dimensional phonon transport. From an applied perspective, the demonstrated enhancement of electron-phonon coupling in ultrathin membranes has direct implications for the design and thermal engineering of cryogenic devices, where controlling the rate at which electrons exchange energy with their surroundings is essential for optimizing detector sensitivity, thermal isolation, and overall device performance at very low temperatures.

# Understanding the Kelvin Scale

The Kelvin is the base unit of temperature in the International System of Units (SI), and it holds a special place in science because it is an *absolute* temperature scale. Unlike Celsius or Fahrenheit, the Kelvin scale begins at absolute zero—the theoretical point at which all thermal motion of particles ceases. This makes it the preferred standard for physics, chemistry, and engineering applications where precise, meaningful temperature measurements are essential.

## Origins and the Man Behind the Name

The scale is named after William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, a Scottish-Irish physicist who proposed the concept of an absolute thermodynamic temperature scale in 1848. His work laid the foundation for much of modern thermodynamics, and in his honor the unit was named "kelvin" (symbol: K). Notably, the kelvin is written without a degree symbol, distinguishing it from the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.

## Key Reference Points

- **0 K** corresponds to absolute zero (−273.15 °C).
- **273.15 K** equals the freezing point of water (0 °C).
- **373.15 K** equals the boiling point of water (100 °C).

Because the kelvin and the Celsius degree share the same size interval, converting between the two is straightforward: simply add or subtract 273.15.

## Standardization and NIS

Maintaining accurate temperature standards requires the work of national and international standards institutions. Bodies such as national institutes of standards (NIS) help define, calibrate, and verify measurement units so that scientific and industrial results remain consistent worldwide. In 2019, the kelvin was formally redefined in terms of a fixed value of the Boltzmann constant, tying the unit to a fundamental constant of nature rather than to the physical properties of water. This shift reflects the ongoing effort by the global metrology community to make measurement systems more universal, reproducible, and precise.

## Conclusion

From the pioneering ideas of Lord Kelvin to the modern standards upheld by measurement institutions, the Kelvin scale represents one of science's most reliable tools. Its grounding in absolute zero and fundamental physical constants ensures that researchers everywhere speak the same language when it comes to temperature.

---

# Abstract

We report measurements of electron-phonon (e-ph) energy relaxation in thin copper wires deposited on suspended silicon nitride membranes at temperatures between 50 mK and 1 K. By fabricating samples on freestanding membranes of varying thickness (30–500 nm), we systematically investigate how phonon dimensionality influences the e-ph coupling strength and its temperature dependence. The electron temperature is extracted via Johnson noise thermometry and complementary current-heated hot-electron measurements, while the phonon bath is maintained at the substrate temperature. In samples on thick membranes, where phonons remain three-dimensional, we observe the conventional power law P ∝ Tⁿ with n ≈ 5, consistent with bulk e-ph scattering. As the membrane thickness is reduced below the dominant thermal phonon wavelength, we find a systematic reduction of the exponent toward n ≈ 4 and a suppression of the coupling constant, signaling a crossover to quasi-two-dimensional phonon behavior. This dimensional reduction restricts the available phonon phase space and modifies the density of vibrational states participating in energy exchange. We compare our results to theoretical models incorporating quantized flexural and dilatational membrane modes, finding quantitative agreement across the measured temperature and thickness range. These findings clarify the role of reduced dimensionality in electron thermalization and have direct implications for the design of cryogenic radiation detectors, bolometers, and hot-electron devices, where phonon-mediated cooling governs performance at millikelvin temperatures.

---

*Keywords:* electron-phonon coupling, phonon dimensionality, silicon nitride membranes, sub-Kelvin thermometry, cryogenic detectors, thermal transport

# Abstract

**Dimensional Crossover in Electron-Phonon Coupling: Enhanced Interaction Strength and Modified Temperature Scaling in Nanoscale Copper Wires**

We investigate the influence of phonon dimensionality reduction on electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions in copper nanowires as their transverse dimensions approach the dominant phonon wavelength. Using a combination of low-temperature resistivity measurements, thermal conductance spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations incorporating confined phonon modes, we demonstrate a systematic crossover from three-dimensional (3D) to quasi-two-dimensional (2D) phonon behavior in wires with lateral dimensions ranging from 8 to 45 nm. Our results reveal that phonon confinement fundamentally alters both the magnitude and temperature dependence of the e-ph coupling constant.

In the 2D regime, we observe a pronounced enhancement of the effective e-ph interaction strength, with the dimensionless coupling parameter λ increasing by up to 35% relative to bulk values. This enhancement arises from the modified phonon density of states and the reduction of available momentum-relaxation channels under transverse confinement. Critically, the temperature dependence of the e-ph scattering rate transitions from the canonical Bloch-Grüneisen T⁵ scaling characteristic of 3D acoustic phonons to an approximate T³ dependence in the confined regime, consistent with the reduced dimensionality of the phonon phase space. The characteristic crossover temperature scales inversely with wire diameter, in agreement with a confinement-induced modification of the effective Debye temperature.

These findings provide direct evidence that geometric confinement of the lattice, rather than electronic confinement alone, governs transport dissipation in metallic nanostructures. Our work has significant implications for thermal management, quantum coherence lifetimes, and the design of nanoscale interconnects, where phonon engineering offers a viable route to controlling energy relaxation. We further discuss how these dimensional effects must be incorporated into predictive models of resistivity scaling as interconnect dimensions continue to shrink below 20 nm.

---

*Keywords: electron-phonon coupling, phonon confinement, dimensional crossover, copper nanowires, Bloch-Grüneisen scaling, nanoscale transport*

We report the first experimental observation of reduced dimensionality in the phonon spectrum modifying electron-phonon scattering rates in metallic thin films. Copper wires deposited on suspended silicon nitride membranes (30 nm thick) were measured below 0.5 K using magnetoresistance and thermal transport techniques. As temperature decreases, the dominant thermal phonon wavelength exceeds the membrane thickness, driving a crossover from three-dimensional to two-dimensional phonon behavior. We observe a corresponding change in the electron-phonon scattering rate, with the temperature dependence deviating from the conventional T³ bulk prediction toward a weaker power law consistent with a two-dimensional phonon density of states.
